chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Ismail, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Safwan, from Muawiya ibn Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said:

Regarding a man who took twenty-one pebbles and threw them, but one remained, and he did not know which of them was deficient from, he said: 'So let him return and let him throw each one with a pebble.'
If a pebble falls from a man and he does not know which of them it was, he said: 'He should take a pebble from under his feet and throw with it.'
He said: 'And if you throw with a pebble and it falls in a carriage, so repeat in its place. And if it hits a person or a camel, then it falls upon the Jamarat, it will suffice you.'

And he said regarding a man who threw the Jamarat, so he threw the first one with four, and the last two with seven, seven: 'He should return and throw the first one with three, and he would have been freed.'
And if he had thrown the first one with three, and threw the last two with seven, seven, so let him return and let him throw all of them with seven, seven.
And if he had thrown the middle one with three, then threw the other one, so let him throw the middle one with seven.
And if he had thrown the middle one with four, he should return and throw with three.

He said, 'I said, The man reverses in throwing the Jamarat, so he begins with Jamarat al-Aqabah, then the middle, then the great one.' He said: 'He should return and throw the middle, then he would throw Jamarat al-Aqabah, and even if it is the next morning.'

key_terms.جَمْرَةُ الْعَقَبَةِ: Jamarat al-Aqabah (the first and largest pillar)
key_terms.يَنْكُسُ: Yankusu (to reverse or invert the order)

ai.seo_question: What are the rulings for correcting mistakes in the number or order of pebbles thrown at the Jamarat during Hajj?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi details the precise jurisprudential remedies for common errors during the Rami al-Jamarat ritual, such as miscounting pebbles or reversing the order of the pillars. It reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on the validity of Hajj acts based on strict adherence to prescribed forms, distinguishing between minor slips that require simple correction and major deviations necessitating a full repetition. The text underscores the importance of intention and precision in fulfilling the pillar of Hajj, ensuring the ritual's spiritual integrity is maintained despite human error.
